name: Digestive system
description: The alimentary canal from the oesophagus to the rectum, plus the liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.

source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Digestive system
groups.tip: Follow your food: oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, then the rectum. The liver, gallbladder and pancreas all pour their juices into the duodenum.

groups.label: Oesophagus and stomach
groups.tip: Remember Can Fred Bake Pies for the stomach parts in order: cardia, fundus, body and pylorus. The oesophagus pierces the diaphragm at the tenth chest vertebra.

groups.label: Small and large intestine
groups.tip: Dow Jones Industrial gives the small intestine in order: duodenum, jejunum, ileum. For the large intestine, think Can A Tired Dog Stay Relaxed.

groups.label: Accessory organs (and spleen)
groups.tip: The liver makes bile, the gallbladder stores it, and the pancreas adds digestive juices, all flowing into the duodenum. The spleen hides under your left ribs and filters blood.

content.origin: From the Greek words for to carry and to eat. It is the tube that carries what you eat.
content.location: It runs down your neck and chest, behind your windpipe and in front of your spine. It passes through the diaphragm at about the tenth chest vertebra, then joins the stomach.
content.description: A muscular tube about 25 centimetres long that lies flat when empty, like a deflated hose. Its top third has muscle you can control, and its lower third works on autopilot.
content.function: It pushes food down to your stomach in waves of muscle squeezing, called peristalsis. A ring of muscle at the bottom stops stomach contents coming back up.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the eat-sophagus, the eating tube that sits just behind your windpipe.
content.clinical: In reflux disease, called GORD, stomach acid keeps splashing up and burns the lining, causing heartburn. Years of reflux can change the lining and raise the risk of cancer.
content.hint: A narrow tube running down behind the windpipe and through the diaphragm to the top of the food sac.

questions.text: Where does the oesophagus run in your neck and chest?
options: Behind the windpipe, in front of the spine
Inside the sac around the heart
questions.explanation: The food pipe sits behind your windpipe and in front of your spine, squeezed between the two.

questions.text: What is the name for stomach acid flowing back up into the oesophagus again and again?
questions.explanation: In GORD, acid keeps flowing back up from the stomach. It irritates the food pipe and causes heartburn.

content.origin: From the Greek word for throat or opening. Another Greek word, gaster, meaning belly, gives us the word gastric.
content.location: High in your belly on the left, tucked just under the diaphragm. The liver sits to its right, the spleen behind and to its left, and the pancreas behind it.
content.description: A J-shaped muscular bag with four parts: cardia, fundus, body and pylorus. When it is empty, its lining folds into ridges, like a crumpled balloon.
content.function: It stores food and churns it with acid into a thick soup called chyme. It makes intrinsic factor, which you need to absorb vitamin B12, and lets food out slowly into the small intestine.
content.mnemonic: Can Fred Bake Pies? This gives the four parts in order: cardia, fundus, body and pylorus.
content.clinical: A peptic ulcer is a raw sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum. Most are caused by a germ called Helicobacter pylori, or by painkillers like ibuprofen.
content.hint: A J-shaped bag under the left dome of the diaphragm, between the food pipe and the first loop of small intestine.

questions.text: Which substance made by the stomach helps you absorb vitamin B12?
questions.explanation: The stomach makes intrinsic factor. It travels with vitamin B12 so the ileum can absorb it later.

questions.text: Which part of the stomach is the dome that rises above where the food pipe enters?
questions.explanation: The fundus is the rounded dome at the top of the stomach, sitting above the cardia where food comes in.

content.origin: From the Latin for twelve. Early anatomists said it was about twelve finger-widths long.
content.location: The first part of the small intestine, starting where the stomach ends. It curves around the head of the pancreas, and most of it is fixed to the back wall of your belly.
content.description: A C-shaped tube about 25 centimetres long, in four parts. Bile and pancreatic juice pour in through one small opening, the major duodenal papilla.
content.function: It mixes acid food from the stomach with bile and pancreatic juice. The juice carries bicarbonate, which neutralises the acid so digestion can carry on.
content.mnemonic: Duodenum sounds like dozen, and it is twelve finger-widths long. It is the first stop after the stomach.
content.clinical: Most duodenal ulcers form in the first part, where acid food lands first. An ulcer here can bleed or burst through the wall.
content.hint: The short C-shaped first loop of small intestine, wrapped around the head of a soft gland.

questions.text: Which organ's head sits inside the C-shaped curve of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas nestles inside the C-shaped loop of the duodenum.

questions.text: Which two juices enter the duodenum through one small opening, the major papilla?
questions.explanation: The bile duct and the main pancreatic duct open together here. So bile and pancreatic juice arrive at the same spot.

content.origin: From the Latin word for empty or fasting. Early anatomists usually found this part empty after death.
content.location: The middle part of the small intestine, after the duodenum. Its coils sit mainly in the upper left of your belly, hung from the back wall by a fan-shaped sheet, the mesentery.
content.description: It makes up about the first two-fifths of the small intestine after the duodenum. It is wider, thicker and redder than the ileum, with tall folds packed close together inside.
content.function: This is where you absorb most of the goodness from food: sugars, amino acids and fats. Its folds and tiny finger-like villi give it a huge surface, like a thick bath towel.
content.mnemonic: Dow Jones Industrial gives the order of the small intestine: duodenum, jejunum, ileum.
content.clinical: If someone cannot be fed through the stomach, a feeding tube can go straight into this part. This is called a feeding jejunostomy.
content.hint: The thick-walled, red coils in the upper left, following straight on from the C-shaped first loop.

questions.text: What is the main job of the jejunum?
questions.explanation: The jejunum absorbs most of your nutrients. Its folds and villi give it a huge surface to do this.

questions.text: The name jejunum comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.explanation: Jejunus means empty or fasting. Early anatomists usually found this part empty after death.

content.origin: Probably from the Greek for to roll or twist, because of its many coils. Do not mix it up with the ilium, your hip bone.
content.location: The last part of the small intestine, coiled in the lower right of your belly and pelvis. It ends at the ileocaecal junction, where it opens into the caecum.
content.description: It makes up about the last three-fifths of the small intestine after the duodenum. It is narrower and thinner than the jejunum, with patches of immune tissue called Peyer's patches.
content.function: It soaks up the last nutrients, and its final stretch absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts. A valve at its end lets food into the large intestine and stops it coming back.
content.mnemonic: Ileum with an E is for entrails, your gut. Ilium with an I is for your hip.
content.clinical: Crohn's disease, a long-term inflammation of the gut, most often strikes the end of the ileum. Damage here can leave you short of vitamin B12.
content.hint: The last coils of small intestine in the lower right, opening into the blind pouch at the start of the large bowel.

questions.text: Which vitamin is mainly absorbed at the very end of the ileum?
questions.explanation: The last part of the ileum absorbs vitamin B12, with help from intrinsic factor made in the stomach.

questions.text: Where does the ileum end?
options: At the bend after the duodenum
At the caecum, the start of the large intestine
questions.explanation: The ileum opens into the caecum at the ileocaecal junction. A valve there controls the flow.

content.origin: From the Latin for something attached. Its full name adds vermiform, meaning worm-shaped.
content.location: Low on the right side of your belly. It hangs from the caecum, just below where the small intestine joins, and most often tucks up behind it.
content.description: A narrow tube, closed at one end and usually about six to ten centimetres long, like a small worm. Its wall is packed with immune tissue.
content.function: It has no essential job in digestion, so you can live well without it. It may help gut immunity and store friendly gut bacteria.
content.mnemonic: Find McBurney's point: go one third of the way from the bony bump at the front of your right hip to your belly button.
content.clinical: In appendicitis the appendix gets blocked and inflamed. Pain often starts around the belly button, then moves to the lower right, and surgeons usually remove it.
content.hint: A small worm-like tube hanging from the blind pouch at the start of the large bowel, low on the right.

questions.text: In appendicitis, where does the pain usually move to?
questions.explanation: Pain often starts around the belly button. It then settles in the lower right, over the appendix.

questions.text: The appendix hangs from which part of the large intestine?
questions.explanation: The appendix hangs from the caecum, the blind pouch where the large intestine begins.

synonyms: Large intestine (with the rectum and anal canal)

content.origin: From kolon, the Greek name for the large intestine. Caecum means blind, because it is a dead-end pouch, and sigmoid means shaped like an S.
content.location: It frames your small intestine on three sides. It starts as the caecum low on the right, climbs up, crosses the upper belly, runs down the left and makes an S-bend in the pelvis.
content.description: This model shows the caecum and colon as one piece. Three muscle bands gather the wall into a row of pouches, like a string of puffy cushions, with small fat tags along it.
content.function: It soaks water and salts out of liquid waste, turning it into solid faeces, and moves it on to the rectum. Its bacteria break down fibre and make some vitamin K.
content.mnemonic: Can A Tired Dog Stay Relaxed? This gives the order: caecum, ascending, transverse, descending, sigmoid, then rectum.
content.clinical: Small pouches bulging out of the wall, called diverticular disease, are most common in the sigmoid part. Bowel cancer is common, so a simple stool test is offered from middle age.
content.hint: The wide, pouched tube with three muscle bands, starting as a blind pouch low on the right and framing the coils of small intestine.

questions.text: Which part of the large intestine is the dead-end pouch low on the right?
questions.explanation: Caecum means blind. It is the dead-end pouch where the large intestine begins.

questions.text: What is the main job of the colon?
options: Absorbing water and salts to form faeces
questions.explanation: The colon soaks up water and salts. This turns liquid waste into solid faeces.

questions.text: In which part of the colon is diverticular disease most common?
questions.explanation: Small pouches in the wall are most common in the sigmoid colon, the S-shaped bend in the pelvis.

content.origin: From the Latin for straight intestine. It was named from animals, because in humans it is actually curved.
content.location: Deep in your pelvis, in front of the sacrum and tailbone. It follows on from the sigmoid colon and ends at the anal canal, where a sling of muscle bends it forwards.
content.description: A tube about 12 to 15 centimetres long that follows the curve of the sacrum. Its lower part widens into a roomy storage pouch, the rectal ampulla.
content.function: It holds faeces until you are ready to go. When its wall stretches, you feel the urge to open your bowels.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the rest-um: faeces rest here before leaving through the anal canal.
content.clinical: A doctor can check the rectum and nearby organs, like the prostate, with a gloved finger. Bleeding from the bottom or a change in bowel habit should be checked for bowel cancer.
content.hint: The last part of the large bowel, lying in the pelvis in front of the sacrum and leading down to the exit.

questions.text: The rectum lies in front of which bones?
questions.explanation: The rectum follows the curve of the sacrum and tailbone at the back of the pelvis.

questions.text: What sets off the urge to open your bowels?
questions.explanation: When faeces stretch the rectal wall, nerves send the message that it is time to go.

content.origin: From the Old English word lifer. The Greek word hepar gives us words like hepatic and hepatitis.
content.location: High on the right of your belly, under the right dome of the diaphragm and sheltered by your lower ribs. It stretches across to the left, above the stomach.
content.description: Your largest internal organ, weighing about 1.5 kilograms. It has a big right lobe and a smaller left lobe, and its main vessels and bile ducts enter on its underside.
content.function: It makes bile, processes food-rich blood from the gut, and stores sugar, iron and vitamins. It also makes clotting proteins and breaks down drugs and alcohol.
content.mnemonic: Picture a chemical factory that makes, stores and cleans. It makes bile, stores vitamins and cleans out alcohol.
content.clinical: Cirrhosis is scarring of the liver, often from alcohol, hepatitis or fatty liver. A sick liver can turn the skin and eyes yellow, called jaundice, as bilirubin builds up.
content.hint: The largest organ in the belly, tucked under the right dome of the diaphragm, with a small green sac on its underside.

questions.text: Which of these is a job of the liver?
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile. The gallbladder then stores it until a meal arrives.

questions.text: Where in the belly is most of the liver found?
questions.explanation: Most of the liver sits high on the right, under the diaphragm and protected by your ribs.

content.origin: From the Old English word for bile, plus bladder. The Greek words chole and kystis give terms like cholecystitis, an inflamed gallbladder.
content.location: Tucked under the right lobe of the liver, high on the right of your belly. Its tip sits behind the ninth right rib cartilage, at the edge of your six-pack muscle.
content.description: A pear-shaped bag about seven to ten centimetres long. Its small duct joins the duct from the liver to form the bile duct, which runs to the duodenum.
content.function: It stores bile from the liver and makes it stronger. After a fatty meal, a hormone called CCK makes it squeeze bile into the duodenum to help digest fat.
content.mnemonic: The old rule of Fs for gallstones: female, forty, fertile and fat. But remember, gallstones can happen to anyone.
content.clinical: Gallstones are common. A stone stuck in its small duct causes pain high on the right after fatty meals, and the gallbladder is often removed.
content.hint: A small green pear-shaped bag tucked under the right lobe of the largest organ in the belly.

questions.text: What does the gallbladder do?
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile. The gallbladder stores it and makes it stronger, ready for a fatty meal.

questions.text: Which hormone makes the gallbladder squeeze after a fatty meal?
questions.explanation: When fat reaches the duodenum, it releases CCK. This hormone makes the gallbladder squeeze out bile.

content.origin: From the Greek for all flesh. It is soft all the way through, with no bone or cartilage.
content.location: It lies across the back wall of your upper belly, behind the stomach. Its head sits in the curve of the duodenum and its tail reaches the spleen.
content.description: A soft, bumpy gland about 15 centimetres long, with a head, neck, body and tail. Its main duct runs along the middle and joins the bile duct at the duodenum.
content.function: It sends digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum to break down food. Small clusters of cells called islets release insulin and glucagon to control your blood sugar.
content.mnemonic: Picture a fish lying across the back of your belly, with its head in the duodenum and its tail touching the spleen.
content.clinical: Acute pancreatitis is a very painful inflammation, most often caused by gallstones or alcohol. Type 1 diabetes happens when the insulin-making cells in the islets are destroyed.
content.hint: A soft, fish-shaped gland lying behind the food sac, with its head in the C-shaped loop and its tail near the spleen.

questions.text: Which hormones are made by the islets of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The islets release insulin and glucagon into the blood. Together they keep your blood sugar steady.

questions.text: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Gallstones and alcohol cause most cases of acute pancreatitis.

content.origin: From splen, the Greek name for this organ. An older Latin name, lien, gives the word lienal.
content.location: High on the left of your belly, behind the stomach and under the diaphragm. Your ninth to eleventh ribs protect it, and the tail of the pancreas touches it.
content.description: A soft, purple organ about the size of a fist, with a notched front edge. It is not part of digestion but part of your immune system.
content.function: It filters your blood, removing old red blood cells and recycling their iron. It also helps fight infection and stores some blood cells and platelets.
content.mnemonic: Count the odd numbers one to eleven: about one by three by five inches, about seven ounces, lying under ribs nine to eleven.
content.clinical: A hard blow to the lower left ribs can split the spleen, causing dangerous bleeding inside. People without a spleen catch serious infections more easily and need extra vaccines.
content.hint: A fist-sized purple organ under the lower left ribs, behind the food sac, touched by the tail of a soft gland.

questions.text: What is a main job of the spleen?
options: Removing old red blood cells from the blood
questions.explanation: The spleen filters your blood. It removes worn-out red blood cells and recycles their iron.

questions.text: Why is the spleen at risk when someone takes a blow to the lower left ribs?
options: It sits under ribs nine to eleven and can split
It is behind the right kidney
It is attached to the appendix
questions.explanation: The spleen lies right under the ninth to eleventh left ribs. A hard blow can split it and cause serious bleeding.
